results.prompt: Explain this result in plain language.

result.text: With the same launch on Mars, weaker gravity keeps the rover airborne longer and lets it travel farther and reach a higher peak than in the Earth reference. The measured impact speed is lower on Mars; this model uses uniform gravity and disables drag, and it does not model suspension, tires, or drivetrain. To test the effect of launch angle, change only the ramp angle and compare the resulting trajectory.

results.prompt: Why is this result different from Earth?

result.text: Mars has weaker gravity than Earth, so the rover stays airborne longer and rises higher, traveling farther before landing. With drag disabled and the same launch settings, its impact speed is slightly lower; the model also omits suspension, tire grip, and drivetrain effects. To isolate gravity’s role, compare the worlds while changing only the world setting and keeping the launch settings fixed.

results.prompt: How do launch angle and drag change the flight?

result.text: Launch angle divides the fixed launch speed between upward and forward motion, shaping how high and far the projectile travels; drag, when enabled, opposes its motion and alters the path. In this Mars run, drag is off, and the measured flight lasted {flightTimeS}, reached {peakHeightM}, and covered {rangeM}. To isolate the effects, vary the angle while holding speed, release height, and world fixed, then enable drag at the same angle and compare.

results.prompt: What sets the pendulum’s period?

result.text: For a pendulum with small swings, period is set mainly by its length and the local gravity: a longer pendulum swings more slowly, while stronger gravity makes it swing faster. In this Earth setup, the bob’s mass does not set the ideal period; the measured period is shown here. Try changing only the length and compare the period, keeping the world and starting angle fixed.

results.prompt: Does mass affect this experiment, and why?

result.text: For this pendulum, bob mass does not set the ideal period: the gravitational force and the bob’s resistance to acceleration both increase with mass, so they cancel. In your Moon setup, length and starting angle determine the motion; the measured period is available here. Try changing only the bob mass while keeping the length and starting angle fixed to test the model.

results.prompt: How do speed and shape affect drag?

result.text: Drag rises with the square of airflow speed, while shape changes how strongly the flow resists the object; a plate has a higher drag coefficient than a sphere in this model. For the current sphere setup, the calculated reference drag is linked to its dynamic pressure and the chosen area. Try changing only wind speed while keeping the object and area fixed to see how drag responds.

results.prompt: Why is the drag force zero here?

result.text: Drag depends on the surrounding gas density, so the Moon’s vacuum model gives zero drag even though a wind speed is set; this wind-tunnel value is a calculated reference force, not a CFD measurement. As a controlled test, keep the sphere, wind speed, and reference area fixed and switch to a world with an atmosphere; no Earth comparison is available in this run.

results.prompt: How does gravity affect the fall?

result.text: Gravity accelerates the released object downward; with weaker gravity, it takes longer to fall and reaches a lower impact speed from the same height. In this Mars setup, both the fall time and impact speed differ from the matched Earth run in those directions. To isolate gravity, compare worlds while keeping drop height, mass, and drag setting unchanged.

results.prompt: Where does the bounce energy go?

result.text: During impact, some motion energy is converted into deformation, heat, sound, and internal vibrations; this ideal bounce model represents that loss through the coefficient of restitution but does not track where the energy goes. In this Titan setup, the measured rebound retains about half the energy, as reflected by the rebound height and energy-retention metrics.
